deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes Euler's discussion of the 'paradox' raised in §§X–XI. A vertical load below π²Ekk/a² produces no bending at all; at that value the bent form becomes possible, and above it the bend grows with the load. Euler says this 'is actually the case in columns', so it is not merely a curiosity of pure theory. In modern terms this is bifurcation of equilibrium: below the critical load the bent solution is imaginary, at the critical load it is zero, and above it it is real.

§XII draws the consequences of the critical load P_cr = π²Ekk/a². Here Ekk is the 'moment de roideur', i.e. the bending stiffness EI, and a is the height.
(i) Taller columns carry less, which agrees with experience.
(ii) The carrying capacity varies as 1/a². So a column twice as tall, of the same material and thickness, carries one quarter of the load.
(iii) Suppose the stiffness is proportional to the cube of the diameter. Then for column (a, d, p) and column (A, D, P) we get p : P = d³/a² : D³/A², hence P = a²D³ p/(A²d³). This scaling law lets one compare columns by both height and thickness.

§XIII tries to give a feel for the absolute size of the critical load. Clamp the column at the base and apply a horizontal force F = π²Ekk/a² at the top. §VIII gives the small-deflection tip displacement of a cantilever as Dδ = F a³/(3Ekk). Substituting gives Dδ = (π²/3)a ≈ 3⅓ a, which is absurd. As the next page explains, this shows that the linearized theory breaks down: the true large deflection would be much smaller, but still enormous. So the vertical load a column can bear is very large compared with a horizontal one.
errors: Conditional scaling with the cube of the diameter. For a solid circular cylinder the bending stiffness EI scales as d⁴, not d³. The correct law is therefore P ∝ D⁴/A², not D³/A². Euler states the cube law only hypothetically ('si le moment de roideur est proportionnel au cube'). It reflects the then-current uncertainty about how stiffness depends on thickness, a d³ law being appropriate for plates of fixed width.

Possible mismatch of end conditions in §XIII. The §VIII deflection Fa³/(3Ekk) is for a column clamped at the base with a free top. With the same Ekk, the critical load of a clamped–free column is π²Ekk/(4a²); π²Ekk/a² corresponds to a column with both ends pinned (or to a different convention for a). If the boundary conditions are mismatched, the illustrative figure π²a/3 is overstated by a factor of 4. Even then it would be about 0.82a, still a huge deflection, so the qualitative point stands. Whether Euler's a here is the full length of a pinned column needs checking against §XV and Fig. 2; unsure.
Using a linear, small-deflection formula at a large load is acknowledged by Euler himself on the next page, so this is not an error.

ideas.what: Critical (buckling) load π²Ekk/a²; below it no deflection, above it a bent equilibrium exists; the 'imaginary inflexion' explanation
ideas.modern_name: Euler buckling load; bifurcation of equilibrium
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum de curvis elasticis (1744); E238

ideas.what: Critical load inversely proportional to the square of the length
Scaling law for different heights and diameters under the assumption stiffness ∝ d³
ideas.modern_name: Similarity scaling of buckling load (correctly ∝ d⁴/L² for circular sections)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (with the incorrect d³ hypothesis); correct d⁴ via the moment of inertia of a section, standard by the 19th century
ideas.where_published: E238 §XII; Euler revisits columns in later papers (e.g., E508–E510, 1778)

ideas.what: Comparing the critical vertical load with the deflection the same force would cause horizontally, to show the linear theory breaks down
ideas.modern_name: Limits of small-deflection (linearized) beam theory; need for the elastica large-deflection solution

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard and well-documented consequences of the Euler load, already discussed by Truesdell and Timoshenko, including the d³ hypothesis. Nothing on this page appears to be missing from the literature.
